Surah "al-Balad" is Meccan by consensus. It has twenty verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

﴿Nay, I swear by this city﴾ (90:1)

It is permissible for the "lā" here to be superfluous (zā'idah, extra), as was mentioned in ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] (see vol. 19, p. 90). This is the view of al-Akhfash, meaning "I swear" (uqsimu), because He says ﴿by this city﴾ and He has indeed sworn by it in His words ﴿and this secure city﴾ [al-Tin: 3]. So how can the oath by it be denied when He has sworn by it? The poet said:

"I remembered Layla, and passion overtook me, and the core of my heart almost does not break (yataqatta')"

That is, "yataqatta'" (it breaks). Here the letter "lā" is used as a connective (silah). From the same usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], in support of His saying in [Sad]: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Sad: 75].

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Ibn Kathir read ﴿la-uqsimu﴾ without an alif after the lam, affirmatively. Al-Akhfash also permitted that it means "alā" (indeed, unquestionably). It has also been said that it is not a negation of the oath; rather it is like the Arabs' saying: "No, by Allah, I did not do such a thing," "No, by Allah, it was not so," and "No, by Allah, I will surely do such a thing."

It has also been said that it is a true negation, and the meaning is: "I do not swear by this city" if you were not in it, after your departure from it. This was related by Makki. Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid that he said: "Nay" is a refutation of them. This is the choice of Ibn al-'Arabi, because he said: "As for the one who said it is a refutation, that is a view that has no rebuttal, because the meaning is sound through it, the wording is secure, and the intended sense is established. It is a refutation of the words of those who denied the Resurrection, and then the oath begins."

Al-Qushayri said: "His saying 'nay' is a refutation of what the human being mentioned in this surah imagined, the one deceived by the world, meaning: the matter is not as he supposes, that no one will have power over him." Then the oath begins.

"Al-balad" (the city) is Makkah, upon which they agreed. That is, "I swear by the sacred city in which you are," because of your honour before Me and My love for you. Al-Wasiti said: that is, "We swear to you by this city which you have honoured by your presence in it alive, and by your blessing in it dead," meaning Madinah. The first view is more correct, because the surah was revealed in Makkah by consensus.

This refers to the future, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [[Qur'an 39:30.]]. Its like is widespread [[In some copies of the original: (common).]] in the speech of the Arabs. You say to one whom you promise honor and gifts: "You are honored and beloved." It is also widespread in the speech of God, because future states are with Him like the present and witnessed, and it suffices you as a decisive proof that it refers to the future, and that interpreting it as the present is impossible: the surah is agreed to be Meccan, before the Conquest. Mansur narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿And you are a lawful place [ḥill]﴾ that he said: "Whatever you do in it, you are in ḥill (lawfulness)." Similarly Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was made lawful for him on the day he entered Mecca that he might kill whomever he wished, so he killed Ibn Khatal [[He was 'Abdullah, who was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and Abu Barzah al-Aslami killed him by the command of the Messenger, may God's blessings be upon him.]], Maqis ibn Subabah, and others." And it was not made lawful for anyone among the people to kill anyone in it after the Messenger of God ﷺ. As-Suddi narrated, saying: "You are lawful [to act] against whoever fights you, that you may kill him." Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was made lawful for him for an hour of a day, then it was closed and made forbidden until the Day of Resurrection, and that was the day of the Conquest of Mecca." It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: [Indeed God made Mecca sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred until the Hour rises. It was not made lawful for anyone before me, nor is it lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day] — the hadith. It has already been mentioned in the surah "al-Ma'idah." Ibn Zayd said: "No one was lawful in it except the Prophet ﷺ." It was also said: "And you are residing in it, and it is your abode." It was also said: "And you are good in it, and I am pleased with you in it." The lexicographers mentioned that it is said: a man is ḥill, ḥalal, and muḥill; and a man is ḥaram and muḥill; and a man is ḥaram and muḥrim. Qatadah said: "You are ḥill in it: you are not sinful." It was also said: it is praise of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: you do not commit in this city what is forbidden for you to commit, out of your knowledge of the right of this House, unlike the polytheists who commit disbelief in God in it. That is: I swear by this sacred House whose sanctity you know, so you dwell in it, honoring it, not committing in it what is forbidden to you. Shurahbil ibn Sa'd said: "And you are ḥill in this city," that is, lawful; that is, they consider Mecca sacred, so that they do not kill game in it or cut a tree in it with a ma'ḍad [[To cut a tree or other things: to cut it with a ma'ḍad, and the ma'ḍad is a sword used for cutting trees.]], yet despite this they consider it lawful to expel you and kill you.

Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: ﴿And the begetter﴾ is Adam, upon him be peace. ﴿And what he begot﴾ means what descended from his offspring. He swore by them because they are the most wondrous of what Allah the Exalted created upon the earth, owing to the clarity, speech and reasoning that are in them, and among them are the prophets and those who call to Allah the Exalted. It was also said: this is an oath by Adam and the righteous among his descendants, and as for [[In some copies of the original: (wa-amma al-talihun).]] those who are not righteous, they are like beasts.

It was said: the begetter is Abraham, and ﴿what he begot﴾ is his descendants. This was stated by Abu 'Imran al-Jawni. Then it is possible that he means all of his descendants, and it is possible that he means the Muslims among his descendants.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿ma﴾ is used here in the sense of ﴿man﴾ (for people), as in His saying ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], and as in His saying ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl: 3], for He is the Creator of the male and the female.

It was also said: ﴿ma﴾ together with what follows it is in the position of a verbal noun, meaning ﴿by the begetter and his begetting﴾, as in His saying: ﴿By the heaven and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5].

Ikrimah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿the begetter﴾ means the one to whom a child is born, and ﴿what he begot﴾ means the barren one to whom no child is born. This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas. On this reading, ﴿ma﴾ is a negation. This is far-fetched and cannot be sound except by supposing an omitted relative pronoun, meaning ﴿by the begetter and him who begot not﴾, and this is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians.

It was said: it is a general statement covering every begetter and every begotten one. This was stated by 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, and its meaning was also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. This is the view preferred by al-Tabari.

Al-Mawardi said: it is possible that ﴿the begetter﴾ refers to the Prophet ﷺ, because of his prior mention, and ﴿what he begot﴾ refers to his community, due to his saying, upon him be peace: [Indeed I am to you in the position of a father; I teach you]. So He swore by him and by his community after He had sworn by his city, in exaggeration of honoring him, upon him be peace.

Here the oath ends, and this is its answer. God may swear by whatever He wills of His creatures, to magnify them, as has been mentioned earlier. "Al-insan" here means the son of Adam. "Fi kabad" means in hardship and toil, from the struggle of this world. The root meaning of kabad is hardship. From it comes takabbada al-laban (the milk became thick, coagulated and firm). From it also comes al-kabid (the liver), because it is blood that has become thick and firm. It is said: kabadtu hadha al-amr (I endured the hardship of this matter), meaning I bore its difficulty. Labid said:

O eye, why did you not weep for Arbad when we rose and the adversaries rose in kabad (struggle)?

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "fi kabad" means in hardship and fatigue. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: in hardship from his carrying, his birth, his nursing, the growth of his teeth, and other of his conditions. 'Ikrimah narrated from him, saying: standing upright in his mother's womb. Al-kabad also means evenness and straightness. Thus this is a favour bestowed upon him in his creation. God, may His praise be exalted, did not create any creature in its mother's womb except lying face downward, except the son of Adam, who is upright in an upright posture. This is the view of al-Nakha'i, Mujahid and others. Ibn Kaysan said: his head is upright in his mother's womb, and when God permits him to come out of his mother's womb, He turns his head toward his mother's legs.

Al-Hasan said: he endures the calamities of this world and the hardships of the Hereafter. Also from him: he endures gratitude in times of ease and endures patience in times of hardship, since he is never free of one of the two. Ibn 'Umar narrated this too. Yaman said: God has not created any creature that endures what the son of Adam endures, and yet he is the weakest of creatures.

Our scholars said: the first thing he endures is the cutting of his navel cord. Then, when he is swaddled with swaddling clothes and tightly bound, he endures constriction and exhaustion. Then he endures nursing, and if he misses it he is lost. Then he endures the growth of his teeth and the movement of his tongue. Then he endures weaning, which is harder than a slap. Then he endures circumcision, pains and griefs. Then he endures the teacher and his assault, the disciplinarian and his correction, and the master and his awe. Then he endures the burden of marriage and the haste in it [[In a copy of the original text and in the margin of al-Jamal: "Then he endures the burden of marriage and haste in it, and the marrying."]]. Then he endures the burden of children, servants and soldiers. Then he endures the burden of houses and the building of palaces. Then old age and decrepitude, and the weakness of knee and foot, amid calamities whose enumeration is great and misfortunes whose recounting is long: headache, toothache, molar pain, eye inflammation, the distress of debt, dental pain, and earache. He endures trials in wealth and person, such as beating and imprisonment. No day passes over him without his suffering hardship in it, and he endures nothing but difficulty. Then death after all of that, then the questioning of the angel, the crushing and darkness of the grave, then resurrection and being presented before God, until he comes to his final abode, either in Paradise or in the Fire.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil﴾. If the matter were up to him, he would not have chosen these hardships. This indicates that he has a Creator who arranged him and decreed these conditions upon him, so let him comply with His command.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-insan" here is Adam. "Fi kabad" means in the middle of the sky.

Al-Kalbi said: this was revealed concerning a man from the Banu Jumah, who was called Abu al-Ashaddayn [[Thus in the copies of the original. In al-Kashshaf, Ruh al-Ma'ani, al-Baydawi and al-Tha'labi: Abu al-Ashad.]]. He would take a Ukazi hide, place it under his feet, and say: whoever removes me from it will get such-and-such. Ten men would pull it until it tore, yet his feet would not move. He was among the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ, and concerning him was revealed: ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ [al-Balad: 5], meaning because of his strength. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "fi kabad" means strong, that is, strong in build, and he was among the strongest men of Quraysh. Likewise Rukanah ibn Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, who was a proverb for courage and might.

It was also said: "fi kabad" means brave of heart, hard of liver, despite the weakness of his creation and the lowliness of his origin. Ibn 'Ata': in darkness and ignorance. Al-Tirmidhi: neglecting what concerns him, occupied with what does not concern him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 90, verses 5–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ That is, does the son of Adam suppose that Allah, mighty and majestic, will never punish him?

(He says, "I have squandered") that is, "I have spent."

("wealth in abundance") that is, much accumulated wealth. "Does he think" means "does he suppose."

("that no one has seen him") that is, that no one has witnessed him; rather, Allah, mighty and majestic, knew this about him. So he was lying in his saying "I have squandered," for he had not spent it.

Abu Hurayrah narrated: The servant will be made to stand, and it will be said, "What did you do with the wealth that I provided you?" He will say, "I spent it and gave its zakah." It will be said, "You only did that so that it would be said, 'He is generous,' and that has been said." Then he will be ordered to the Fire.

It is narrated from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "You will be questioned about your wealth: from where did you gather it, and how did you spend it?"

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Abu al-Ashaddayn used to say, "I spent much wealth in opposition to Muhammad," and he was lying in that.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal. He committed a sin and asked the Prophet ﷺ for a ruling, and he commanded him to make expiation. He said, "My wealth has gone on expiations and expenditures since I entered the religion of Muhammad." This statement of his may be an expression of boasting about what he spent, in which case it is arrogance on his part, or an expression of regret over it, in which case it is remorse on his part.

Abu Ja'far recited (مَالًا لبدا) with the ba' doubled and fatha, as the plural of lubad, like raki' and ruka', sajid and sujjad, shahid and shuhhad, and similar forms. Mujahid and Humayd recited with a damma on the ba' and lam, lightened, as the plural of lubud. The rest recited with a damma or kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', lightened, as the plural of lubdah and libdah, which is that which is matted together, meaning abundance. The discussion of this has already passed in surah "al-Jinn" [see vol. 19, p. 22 and following].

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he used to recite (أَيَحْسُبُ) with a damma on the sin in both places. Al-Hasan said: He says, "I have destroyed much wealth; who will call me to account for it? Leave me, I will reckon it." Does he not know that Allah is able to call him to account, and that Allah, mighty and majestic, sees his conduct? Then He enumerated His blessings upon him, saying: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes, with which he sees?﴾ ﴿And a tongue, and two lips?﴾ The meaning is: We did that, and We are able to resurrect him and count what he did.

Abu Hazim said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, said: O son of Adam, if your tongue disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two lips, so close them. If your eye disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two eyelids, so close them. If your private part disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two [parts], so close it."

The shafah (lip): its origin is shafahah, from which the ha' was dropped. Its diminutive is shufayhah, and its plural is shifah. It is also said shafahat and shafawat; the ha' is more analogical, and the waw is more general, by analogy with sanawat. Al-Azhari said: It is said "hadhihi shafatun" in connected speech, and "shafahun" with the ta' and the ha'.

Qatadah said: The blessings of Allah are manifest; He makes you acknowledge them so that you may give thanks.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 90, verses 5–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ That is, does the son of Adam suppose that Allah, mighty and majestic, will never punish him?

(He says, "I have squandered") that is, "I have spent."

("wealth in abundance") that is, much accumulated wealth. "Does he think" means "does he suppose."

("that no one has seen him") that is, that no one has witnessed him; rather, Allah, mighty and majestic, knew this about him. So he was lying in his saying "I have squandered," for he had not spent it.

Abu Hurayrah narrated: The servant will be made to stand, and it will be said, "What did you do with the wealth that I provided you?" He will say, "I spent it and gave its zakah." It will be said, "You only did that so that it would be said, 'He is generous,' and that has been said." Then he will be ordered to the Fire.

It is narrated from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "You will be questioned about your wealth: from where did you gather it, and how did you spend it?"

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Abu al-Ashaddayn used to say, "I spent much wealth in opposition to Muhammad," and he was lying in that.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal. He committed a sin and asked the Prophet ﷺ for a ruling, and he commanded him to make expiation. He said, "My wealth has gone on expiations and expenditures since I entered the religion of Muhammad." This statement of his may be an expression of boasting about what he spent, in which case it is arrogance on his part, or an expression of regret over it, in which case it is remorse on his part.

Abu Ja'far recited (مَالًا لبدا) with the ba' doubled and fatha, as the plural of lubad, like raki' and ruka', sajid and sujjad, shahid and shuhhad, and similar forms. Mujahid and Humayd recited with a damma on the ba' and lam, lightened, as the plural of lubud. The rest recited with a damma or kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba', lightened, as the plural of lubdah and libdah, which is that which is matted together, meaning abundance. The discussion of this has already passed in surah "al-Jinn" [see vol. 19, p. 22 and following].

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he used to recite (أَيَحْسُبُ) with a damma on the sin in both places. Al-Hasan said: He says, "I have destroyed much wealth; who will call me to account for it? Leave me, I will reckon it." Does he not know that Allah is able to call him to account, and that Allah, mighty and majestic, sees his conduct? Then He enumerated His blessings upon him, saying: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes, with which he sees?﴾ ﴿And a tongue, and two lips?﴾ The meaning is: We did that, and We are able to resurrect him and count what he did.

Abu Hazim said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, said: O son of Adam, if your tongue disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two lips, so close them. If your eye disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two eyelids, so close them. If your private part disputes with you concerning what I have forbidden to you, then I have helped you against it with two [parts], so close it."

The shafah (lip): its origin is shafahah, from which the ha' was dropped. Its diminutive is shufayhah, and its plural is shifah. It is also said shafahat and shafawat; the ha' is more analogical, and the waw is more general, by analogy with sanawat. Al-Azhari said: It is said "hadhihi shafatun" in connected speech, and "shafahun" with the ta' and the ha'.

Qatadah said: The blessings of Allah are manifest; He makes you acknowledge them so that you may give thanks.

Its meaning is the two paths: the path of good and the path of evil, that is, We made both clear to him through the messengers We sent. And najd is the road in an elevated place. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others. Qatadah narrated, saying: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'O people, the two najds are only: the najd of good and the najd of evil. So did We not make the najd of evil dearer to you than the najd of good?'" It is narrated from 'Ikrimah that he said: "The two najds are the two breasts." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, because the two breasts are like the two paths to the life of the child and its sustenance. So najd means height, its plural is nujud, and from it the name "Najd" was given, because of its elevation above the lowland of Tihamah. Thus the two najds are the two high roads. Imru' al-Qays said:

"A party of them cuts off the valley of Nakhla,
and another of them cuts through the height of Kabkab."

[[As in the original and in the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays. In al-Lisan (entry: najd):

"At morning, when they set out, they asked about the valley of Nakhla."

Al-jaziʿ: the one who cuts. Batn Nakhla: a place between Makkah and al-Ta'if. Kabkab: the red mountain you find behind you when you stand at 'Arafah.]]

﴿Then he has not attempted the steep path.﴾ That is: why did he not spend his wealth, which he claims he spent in hostility toward Muhammad, why did he not spend it to attempt the steep path so that he would be safe? 

Iqtihām (storming into something) means throwing oneself into a matter without deliberation. It is said: *qahama fi al-amr quhūman*, meaning he threw himself into the matter without deliberation. *Qahhama al-faras fārisahu taqhīman ʿalā wajhihi* means the horse threw its rider on his face, when it cast him off. *Taqhīm al-nafs fi al-shay'* means plunging oneself into something without deliberation. *Al-quhma* (with a dammah) means destruction, and a severe year. It is said: *aṣābat al-aʿrāb al-quhma*, meaning the Bedouins were struck by a severe year, when drought befell them, so they entered the settled lands (al-rīf). *Al-quham* means difficult roads.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: *lā* is mentioned only once, and the Arabs rarely use *lā* alone with the past tense in such a position, unless they repeat it elsewhere in the speech, as in God's words ﴿So he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] and ﴿No fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. They used it singly only because the end of the speech indicates its meaning. Thus His words ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17] may stand in place of the repetition, as if He had said: ﴿So he did not attempt the steep path, nor did he believe﴾. It was also said that it functions as a supplication, like the saying *lā najā wa-lā salima*, meaning "may he not be saved, nor safe."

﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said: everywhere God says ﴿And what will make you know?﴾, He has informed of it, and everywhere He says ﴿And what will make you know?﴾ He has not informed of it. He also said: the meaning of ﴿So he did not attempt the steep path﴾ is that he did not attempt the steep path, like the verse of Zuhayr:

*"And he folded his side over a hidden intention, / So he neither revealed it nor advanced."*

(*Al-kashh* is the flank; *mustakinna* is an intention he concealed within himself.)

That is, he did not reveal it and did not advance. Al-Mubarrad and Abū ʿAlī said likewise: *fa-lā* here means *lam*. Al-Bukhārī reported from Mujāhid that the meaning is that he did not attempt the steep path in this world, so there is no need for repetition. Then He explained the steep path and its climbing, saying ﴿freeing a slave﴾ and so forth, thus specifying forms of wealth-based acts of nearness to God.

Ibn Zayd and a group of exegetes said: the meaning of the speech is an interrogative of denial, its implied sense being: ﴿Why did he not attempt the steep path?﴾ or ﴿Would that he had attempted the steep path!﴾ The meaning is: why did he not spend his wealth on freeing slaves and feeding the hungry, so that he might cross the steep path with it, which would have been better for him than spending it in hostility toward Muhammad ﷺ.

Then it was said: attempting the steep path here is a parable, meaning: did he take upon himself the great burdens by spending his wealth in obedience to his Lord and in faith in Him? This fits only the view of those who take ﴿So he did not attempt the steep path﴾ as a supplication, meaning: may he who does not spend his wealth in such and such not be saved nor safe.

It was also said: He likened the greatness, weight and severity of sins to a steep path. When one frees a slave and does righteous deeds, his case is like that of one who attempted the steep path, which is the sins that harm him, injure him and weigh him down.

Ibn ʿUmar said: this steep path is a mountain in Hell.

From Abū Rajāʾ, who said: we have been told that the ascent of the steep path takes seven thousand years, and its descent seven thousand years.

Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: it is a severe steep path in the Fire, before the Bridge (al-jisr), so storm it through obedience to God.

Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī said: it is the Path (al-ṣirāṭ), laid over Hell like the edge of a sword, three thousand years long, with level stretches, ascents and descents. Its crossing for the believer is like the time between the afternoon prayer and the night prayer. It was also said: its crossing for him is as long as it takes to pray an obligatory prayer.

It is narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ that he said: indeed, behind us is a steep path, and the people most saved from it are the lightest of load.

It was also said: the Fire itself is the steep path. Abū Rajāʾ reported from al-Ḥasan, who said: we have been told that no Muslim frees a slave except that it becomes his ransom from the Fire.

From ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, who said: whoever frees a slave, God, Mighty and Majestic, frees with every limb of it a limb of his.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayra, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: [Whoever frees a slave, God frees with every limb of it a limb of his from the Fire, even his private part for her private part.]

In al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Umāma and others among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: [Any Muslim man who frees a Muslim man, it will be his ransom from the Fire; every limb of his will repay a limb of his. And any Muslim woman who frees a Muslim woman, it will be her ransom from the Fire; every limb of hers will repay a limb of hers.] He said: this is a hadith that is ḥasan, ṣaḥīḥ, gharīb.

It was also said: the steep path is his deliverance from the terror of the Gathering (al-ʿarḍ).

Qatādah and Kaʿb said: it is a Fire before the Bridge.

Al-Ḥasan said: by God, it is a severe steep path: a person's striving against his own self, his desire, and his enemy Satan.

Someone recited:

*"I have been afflicted with four who shoot me / with arrows, having set a snare for me:*
*Iblīs, the world, my own self, and desire, / from where can I hope for an escape from among them?*
*O Lord, help me with Your pardon, for I / have become one who hopes for no one but You."*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 90, verse 12:

There is an ellipsis in it, meaning: "And what will make you know what the steep path (iqtiham al-'aqabah) is?" This is an exaltation of adherence to the matter of the religion, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he may be informed of the crossing of the steep path (al-'aqabah). Al-Qushayri said: To take the 'aqabah as the 'aqabah of Jahannam (Hell) is far-fetched, since no one in this world has crossed the 'aqabah of Jahannam, unless it is taken to mean: "Why did he not make himself such that it is possible for him to cross the 'aqabah of Jahannam tomorrow." Al-Bukhari chose the view of Mujahid: that he did not cross the 'aqabah in this world. Ibn al-'Arabi said: He only chose that because after this, in the second verse, He says: "And what will make you know what the steep path is?" Then He says in the third verse: "The freeing of a neck," and in the fourth verse: "Or feeding on a day of hunger," then He says in the fifth verse: "an orphan near of kin," then He says in the sixth verse: "or a needy person in misery." These deeds are only performed in this world. The meaning: he did not, in this world, do that which would make it easy for him to traverse the steep path in the Hereafter.

**Three issues arise here.**

**The first issue** concerns God's words, ﴿freeing a neck﴾, [and] ﴿freeing it﴾: [this means] delivering it from captivity. It is also said [it means] from enslavement. In a hadith [it is related]: "Freeing the neck is helping someone pay its price," from the hadith of al-Bara' (ra). It has been mentioned previously in the commentary on Surah Bara'ah [see vol. 8, p. 183]. *Fakk* (freeing) means removing a shackle, and enslavement is a shackle. The enslaved person is called a *raqabah* (neck) because, through enslavement, he is like a captive bound by the neck. The neck itself is called *fakk*, just as the release of a captive from captivity is called *fakk*. Hassan said:

"How many a captive we freed without ransom,
and shorn forelocks whose masters we were."

'Uqbah ibn 'Amir al-Juhani narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever frees a believing neck, it will be his ransom from the Fire." Al-Mawardi said: "It is also possible that he meant the freeing of his own neck and the deliverance of his soul by avoiding sins and performing acts of obedience. The report does not preclude this interpretation, and it is closer to the correct view."

**The second issue** concerns God's words, ﴿a neck﴾. Asbagh said: "A disbelieving slave of high price is better in manumission than a believing slave of low price, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, when he was asked which necks are best: 'The most expensive in price and the most precious to their owners.'" Ibn al-Arabi said: "What is meant in this hadith is [a slave] from among the Muslims, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever frees a Muslim man' and 'whoever frees a believing neck.'" What Asbagh mentioned was a slip [[Thus in the originals and in Ibn al-Arabi. It may be *al-marrah* from *al-wahl*, meaning error. *Hala ila al-shay'* (with fatha) yahalu (with kasra) halan (with sukun) means his mind went toward it. It may also mean an error or an oversight.]], and he only considered the reduction of wealth, whereas considering the freed person's dedication to worship and devotion to monotheism is preferable.

**The third issue** is that manumission and charity are among the best deeds. According to Abu Hanifah, manumission is better than charity, while according to his two companions, charity is better. The verse is more clearly in support of Abu Hanifah's view, since manumission is placed before charity. On al-Sha'bi, regarding a man who has surplus money for expenditure, [it was asked] whether he should give it to a relative or free a neck. He said: "The neck is better, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever frees a neck, Allah frees with each limb of it a limb of his from the Fire.'"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 90, verse 14–16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾, i.e., on a day of famine (majaʻah). Al-saghab (hunger) is hunger, and al-saghib is one who is hungry. Al-Hasan recited ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, a near of kin﴾ (ṭaʻām fī yawm dhā masghabah) with an alif in dhā, and Abu ʻUbaydah recited in verse:

"Had you been a neighbour [[As in the original manuscripts. He means: had you been a neighbour who truly upheld the rights of neighbourhood, this would not have happened.]] O son of Qays ibn ʻĀṣim...
you would not have spent the night full while your neighbour was hungry."

Feeding people with food is a virtue, and it is more excellent when it is given to someone suffering from saghab, which is hunger. Al-Nakha'i said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾, "On a day when food is scarce." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Among the things that make mercy obligatory is feeding a hungry Muslim."

(﴿an orphan near of kin﴾), i.e., a relative. It is said: "So-and-so is my near relative (dhū qarābatī) and my kinsman (dhū maqrabatī)." This informs you that charity given to a relative is more excellent than charity given to a non-relative, just as charity given to an orphan who has no guardian is more excellent than charity given to an orphan who has someone to care for him. The lexicographers say: he was called yatīm (orphan) because of his weakness. It is said: yatima al-rajul yatman, when he became weak.

They mention that the orphan among people is one whose father has died, and among animals one whose mothers have died. This has been fully discussed in Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 14, second edition.]]. Some lexicographers say: the yatīm is one whose two parents have died. Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:

"To Allah I complain of the loss of Layla, as the orphan complains to Allah of the loss of his two parents."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾, i.e., one who has nothing, to the point that it is as if he has clung to the dust from poverty, having no shelter but the dust. Ibn ʻAbbas said: he is one cast down on the road who has no house. Mujahid said: he is one whom no clothing or anything else protects from the dust. Qatadah said: he is one with dependants. ʻIkrimah said: the debtor. Abu Sinan said: one afflicted by disability. Ibn Jubayr said: one who has no one. ʻIkrimah related from Ibn ʻAbbas: dhū al-matrabah is one far from his land, meaning the stranger far from his homeland. Abu Hamid al-Kharzanji said: al-matrabah here derives from al-taraybah, which is severity of condition. It is said: "tariba" when one becomes poor. Al-Hudhali said:

"When a guest alighted in our land, we would shed the blood of camels in the dust of hardship."

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and al-Kisa'i recited (fakka) with a fatha on the kaf, as a past-tense verb.

(raqabatan) in the accusative as its object, or (aṭʻama) with a fatha on the hamza and a fatha on the mim, without an alif, also as a past-tense verb, due to His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾, so this is more fitting with fakka and aṭʻama. The rest recited fakku in the nominative, as a verbal noun of fakaktu, with raqabatin in the genitive by annexation. Or iṭʻāmun with a kasra on the hamza, an alif, and a damma on the mim with tanwin, also as a verbal noun. Abu ʻUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because it is an explanation of His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ Then He informed of it, saying: ﴿the freeing of a neck, or feeding.﴾ The meaning: the assault upon the steep path is the freeing of a neck or feeding. Whoever recited in the accusative, it is taken as construed according to the sense, i.e., "he did not free a neck, nor feed on a day of hunger, so how could he cross the steep path?" Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' recited dhā masghabatin in the accusative, as the object of iṭʻām, i.e., they feed one who is in hunger, and yatīman is a substitute for it. The rest recited dhī masghabatin, which is an adjective of yawm. It is also permissible that the accusative recitation is an adjective of the position of the prepositional phrase, since His saying fī yawmin is an adverbial accusative of place, so it would be a description of it according to the sense rather than the wording.

It was also said: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ means he did these deeds while being a believer, then he remained upon his faith until death. Its parallel is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving toward those who repent, believe, do righteousness, and then remain guided﴾ [Taha: 82].

Yahya ibn Sallam said: because they are blessed (mayamin) for their own souls. Ibn Zayd said: because they were taken from the right side of Adam. It was also said: because their station is on the right, as stated by Maymun ibn Mihran.

﴿And those who disbelieved in Our verses﴾, that is, in the Qur'an.

﴿They are the companions of the left hand﴾, that is, they will take their books in their left hands. This was said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. Yahya ibn Sallam said: because they are ill-omened (mashaʾim) for their own souls. Ibn Zayd said: because they were taken from the left side of Adam. Maymun said: because their station is on the left.

I say: what gathers these sayings is that it may be said: the companions of the right hand are the people of Paradise, and the companions of the left hand are the people of the Fire. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the companions of the right—what of the companions of the right? Among lote trees without thorns﴾, and He said: ﴿And the companions of the left—what of the companions of the left? In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ [Al-Waqiʿah: 27–28, 41–42], and what is similar to it.

The meaning of ﴿mu'sadah﴾ is closed, sealed shut. The poet said:

My she-camel yearns for the mountains of Makkah, and between her and them are the gates of Sanʿa, shut fast.
